opening.title: Notes from My Table
opening.body: Things I made, broke and learned to mend became these notes. Read as yourself or someone you play. Tap a name to jump; the links below lead back.

how_to.title: A Deck in Hand
how_to.body: Use a deck to draw its top card. Sneak-use to shuffle. To return a card, hold it in your offhand and sneak-use the deck. Otherwise, keep your offhand clear while handling cards.

how_to.title: Around the Table
how_to.body: Use a loose card on a clear, flat surface to lay it face-down. Use it to flip; sneak-use to rotate. Empty-hand hit picks it up. Hit with a deck to return it; sneak-hit gathers nearby cards.

reading.title: A Little Reading
reading.body: Try one card for a choice, or three for a story. These are prompts, never predictions. Deal blind: hold a deck and aim at a table, then /trigger tarot.action set 5.

sections.title: Major Arcana
sections.intro: Turning points I learned to notice while making a home.

entries.name: The Fool
entries.body: My first shelter had no roof. I remember that valley whenever a plan begins before I know enough. In a story, the first step can be brave and unfinished.

entries.name: The Magician
entries.body: Spare planks became a workbench beside a door. Making starts when I notice what is already in reach. Give a character one useful skill and a reason to try it.

entries.name: The High Priestess
entries.body: There was a room behind the shelves I passed for weeks. Silence can hold something worth learning. Let a character listen before explaining the whole mystery.

entries.name: The Empress
entries.body: The garden did better once I stopped treating every flower as wasted space. Care can make abundance worth having. What would your character leave room to enjoy?

entries.name: The Emperor
entries.body: My first keep had thick walls and one cramped entrance. Order ought to help people live inside it. Ask whose needs a character's rules actually protect.

entries.name: The Hierophant
entries.body: A neighbor taught me to stagger the bricks. Later I found another way. A shared method gives us a start; a good lesson also leaves room for a question.

entries.name: The Lovers
entries.body: We argued over where to build, then spoke about why we wanted a home. This card asks what a character chooses to stand by when affection becomes commitment.

entries.name: The Chariot
entries.body: The junction worked only after I chose where each rail should lead. Resolve is more than pushing harder. Which competing aim could a character bring into line?

entries.name: Strength
entries.body: The horse stopped shying when I put the fence down and waited. Patience took more courage than grabbing the lead. Try giving a strong character a gentle response.

entries.name: The Hermit
entries.body: On the hill, I could hear my own question again. Some problems need a lantern and an evening alone. What understanding would a character bring back to the village?

entries.name: Wheel of Fortune
entries.body: A full wheat chest became an empty one while I built elsewhere. Circumstances turn without asking. Let a character meet a change without calling it a final verdict.

entries.name: Justice
entries.body: I took more iron than I remembered, and the ledger showed it. Fairness began with replacing it. What evidence would change a character's account of a dispute?

entries.name: The Hanged Man
entries.body: The bridge repair stalled until I stopped trying to save my first design. Underneath, the fault looked different. What would I see if I let the old plan wait?

entries.name: Death
entries.body: When we left the old base, I took its crooked door. It could come with us; the life around it could not. I wasn't ready to call the leaving a fresh start.

entries.name: Temperance
entries.body: Too much water ruined my neat little channel. Small adjustments finally let both fields drink. In a reading, ask which different needs could find a workable balance.

entries.name: The Devil
entries.body: I kept mining after I had enough, afraid to leave the next diamond. A useful habit had become a tether. What does a character keep choosing despite its cost?

entries.name: The Tower
entries.body: Lightning caught the wooden spire I had called safe. I stood with the bucket long after the flames went out. What else have I mistaken for certain?

entries.name: The Star
entries.body: After the fire, we repaired the well first. One small useful thing made another possible. Let hope enter a story through something someone chooses to tend.

entries.name: The Moon
entries.body: At the marsh, I mistook a reed's shadow for a waiting mob. Fear and evidence looked alike. Let a character admit uncertainty before making a confident claim.

entries.name: The Sun
entries.body: The courtyard was finished, but the best part was everyone sitting in it. Some joys need no improvement. Give a character a moment they can enjoy without earning more.

entries.name: Judgement
entries.body: The bell brought us together to discuss the wall I had neglected. Owning the failure changed my next choice. What unfinished matter asks a character to answer now?

entries.name: The World
entries.body: The final map showed the railway, farms and homes together. I had forgotten how far we'd come. Let a character recognize completion before inventing another task.

sections.title: Wands
sections.intro: Ideas, bold starts and the effort of carrying them through.

entries.name: Ace of Wands
entries.body: A torch beside the empty plot made me want to build there. An idea begins as an appetite for trying. What small start would give a character's enthusiasm a shape?

entries.name: Two of Wands
entries.body: I marked two possible towers before hauling any stone. Ambition needs a view beyond the next block. Ask how far a character wants this new undertaking to reach.

entries.name: Three of Wands
entries.body: The boats left with our first shipment while I extended the dock. Once work enters the wider world, waiting can be active. What would a character prepare to receive?

entries.name: Four of Wands
entries.body: We hung lanterns on the arch before the road was finished. A milestone deserved its own evening. Let the people who helped make a place feel welcome inside it.

entries.name: Five of Wands
entries.body: Five of us built five different corners. Things improved once we stopped building over one another. A story's rivalry can make room for useful differences.

entries.name: Six of Wands
entries.body: They raised a banner when I finished the bridge. I asked the miners to stand beside me. Recognition feels different when a character names the hands behind the work.

entries.name: Seven of Wands
entries.body: I kept the public path open when the bigger build pressed against it. Some boundaries deserve defending. Which conviction would a character hold despite the objections?

entries.name: Eight of Wands
entries.body: Three messages arrived before I finished answering the first. Suddenly every plan was moving. Give a scene momentum, and ask which response cannot wait until tomorrow.

entries.name: Nine of Wands
entries.body: The patched fence held, though I kept checking it. Experience can protect us and leave us tired. What support would help a character stand watch without standing alone?

entries.name: Ten of Wands
entries.body: My inventory was full of everyone else's errands. I could barely carry home my own tools. A responsible character may need to share the load before taking another task.

entries.name: Page of Wands
entries.body: A new kind of wood sent me sketching doorways all afternoon. Curiosity needn't promise a grand project. Let a character follow an interest far enough to learn its shape.

entries.name: Knight of Wands
entries.body: I rode out to fetch sand and returned with plans for a port. Enthusiasm can outrun its purpose. What would make a character stay once the first excitement wears off?

entries.name: Queen of Wands
entries.body: The workshop filled once I stopped apologizing for my bright banners. Confidence can be hospitable. Give a character enough warmth to encourage someone else's bold idea.

entries.name: King of Wands
entries.body: The settlement began as marks in dirt. It became real when others changed my plan. A leader's vision needs direction and room for people who will live inside it.

sections.title: Cups
sections.intro: The company, feelings and small joys that give a home its warmth.

entries.name: Ace of Cups
entries.body: We found a spring while clearing rubble, and work stopped for a while. Some feelings arrive before their names. Let a character make room for unexpected tenderness.

entries.name: Two of Cups
entries.body: We traded spare tools beside the campfire. Neither of us kept score. I remember how easy it felt to offer something without arranging a debt.

entries.name: Three of Cups
entries.body: Three bowls, three chairs, and nobody talking about the next build. Friendship sometimes needs an evening of its own. Who lets your character laugh without explaining?

entries.name: Four of Cups
entries.body: The soup went cold while I stared at the unfinished wall. I nearly missed the person offering it. Let a character's dissatisfaction hide an invitation worth noticing.

entries.name: Five of Cups
entries.body: The flood took the little dock I loved. Two boats survived on the bank. A character can grieve what went wrong without being asked to overlook what still remains.

entries.name: Six of Cups
entries.body: An old sign still calls our treehouse a castle. I remember the friend who believed it with me. What kindness from the past could a character carry into the present?

entries.name: Seven of Cups
entries.body: Every stall made me imagine a different project. I left with no supplies at all. Possibilities can obscure a real desire; ask which one a character can actually name.

entries.name: Eight of Cups
entries.body: The comfortable base had become a habit. Leaving was harder than building it. What valued thing might a character outgrow without calling it worthless?

entries.name: Nine of Cups
entries.body: Bread, stew, a clean table: I had everything I wanted that evening. Contentment deserves a page too. Let a character enjoy enough without turning it into another target.

entries.name: Ten of Cups
entries.body: Our feast needed extra chairs, and we were glad to make them. Belonging is a joy people keep tending. Ask how a character helps shared happiness last beyond one evening.

entries.name: Page of Cups
entries.body: I meant to draw a pond; the fish became the whole sketch. An odd little feeling can open a new interest. Give a character room to be surprised by their own affection.

entries.name: Knight of Cups
entries.body: I built an elaborate flower arch before asking whether anyone wanted a party. A lovely intention still needs an answer. How could a character make an invitation freely?

entries.name: Queen of Cups
entries.body: At the window, I learned to listen without reaching for my tools. Some feelings need company before solutions. What care can a character offer without taking over?

entries.name: King of Cups
entries.body: A quarrel broke out while we repaired the harbor. I was angry too, but put the hammer down. Let a character feel strongly and still choose how to express it.

sections.title: Swords
sections.intro: Clear thoughts, hard truths and arguments I have had to learn from.

entries.name: Ace of Swords
entries.body: The fault was one missing support, not the whole design. Naming it made the repair possible. Give a character a clear thought that cuts through a tangle of argument.

entries.name: Two of Swords
entries.body: I shut the gate and postponed choosing a route. Neither road went away. What fact or feeling must a character finally admit before an uneasy truce can become a decision?

entries.name: Three of Swords
entries.body: The broken sign carried words I wished I had never said. Repairing the wood was easier. A story can let an honest hurt remain visible without rushing to explain it away.

entries.name: Four of Swords
entries.body: Armor beside the bed meant I could stop for the evening. Leaving a quarrel alone is sometimes useful work. What might a character understand after a quiet interval?

entries.name: Five of Swords
entries.body: I won the argument about the arena and lost my building partner. The empty stands made the cost plain. Ask what a character's victory leaves them unable to celebrate.

entries.name: Six of Swords
entries.body: We crossed the river carrying tools from a failed settlement. Distance did not erase it, but gave us room. A transition can begin before a character feels entirely ready.

entries.name: Seven of Swords
entries.body: I dug a tunnel to avoid a hard conversation at the gate. Cleverness solved the route, not the debt. Who pays for the secret that makes a character's plan so convenient?

entries.name: Eight of Swords
entries.body: Inside my own fence maze, I forgot I had left a gate. A close view can make every limit seem permanent. Let a character inspect an assumption before calling it a wall.

entries.name: Nine of Swords
entries.body: All night I imagined the roof failing again. By morning I could finally tell someone. A worried character's story may change when fear is spoken instead of rehearsed.

entries.name: Ten of Swords
entries.body: The outpost was gone; no repair would save that plan. Admitting it let me put the old sketches down. Give a defeat an ending instead of demanding one more defense.

entries.name: Page of Swords
entries.body: A strange mark in the mine became a question in my notebook. Looking closely is useful; announcing a theory too soon is less so. What could a character check first?

entries.name: Knight of Swords
entries.body: I ran to explain my solution and spoke over the people using it. Certainty had made me careless. Let a character's urgent idea meet the voices it rushes past.

entries.name: Queen of Swords
entries.body: I learned to say which work I could take and which I couldn't. A clear boundary made my help more honest. Can a character be compassionate without disguising the truth?

entries.name: King of Swords
entries.body: At the council, I explained the rule and accepted the same measure myself. Authority asks for open reasoning. What standard would a character apply consistently?

sections.title: Pentacles
sections.intro: Tools, patient work and the care that keeps a place livable.

entries.name: Ace of Pentacles
entries.body: A seed and a patch of soil gave my plans somewhere real to begin. An opportunity needs tending as well as welcome. What practical first step could a character afford?

entries.name: Two of Pentacles
entries.body: While iron smelted, I checked the wheat, then came back to the furnace. Neither task kept my pace. I learned to adjust instead of calling each interruption a failure.

entries.name: Three of Pentacles
entries.body: The mason saw a fault I had missed; the carpenter found its cause. Our workshop improved through shared skills. Let a character value advice they could not supply alone.

entries.name: Four of Pentacles
entries.body: I hid the spare tools under my workshop floor, then wondered why nobody stayed to build. What was I keeping safe: the tools, or my claim on the place?

entries.name: Five of Pentacles
entries.body: Once I needed a warm doorway and didn't know how to ask. Hardship can make help look far away. In a story, who notices the people passing outside the light?

entries.name: Six of Pentacles
entries.body: I stocked the spare-tools chest, let people choose what they needed. Giving carries power. What terms would let a character receive help without surrendering their say?

entries.name: Seven of Pentacles
entries.body: The orchard took longer than my wall, and I couldn't hurry it with more stone. Assessment needs patience. Which part of a character's work needs time or a new approach?

entries.name: Eight of Pentacles
entries.body: My first row of hinges hung crooked; the next row improved. Skill grew through small corrections I could see. Give a character a practice worth their patient attention.

entries.name: Nine of Pentacles
entries.body: In the shade of my own garden, I finally sat down. Care had made a little independence possible. Let a character appreciate a comfort they have learned to sustain.

entries.name: Ten of Pentacles
entries.body: The base holds my old tools beside somebody else's new plans. What lasts should remain useful. Ask what a character's community can leave in good order for newcomers.

entries.name: Page of Pentacles
entries.body: I planted one sapling to see how the space would change. A serious interest can begin with a small trial. What could a character learn by tending something ordinary well?

entries.name: Knight of Pentacles
entries.body: Every morning I check the gates, even the one that never fails. Reliability keeps others safe. When might a character need to examine the routine as well as the fence?

entries.name: Queen of Pentacles
entries.body: Bread, dry boots, and an empty chair made the workshop welcoming. Practical care includes its maker. How could a character offer comfort and keep some for themselves?

entries.name: King of Pentacles
entries.body: A full granary mattered more than its planned grand roof. Stewardship looks beyond display. What resource has a character agreed to keep dependable for others?

sections.title: The Digits
sections.intro: Nine ways a number can lend a character to a scene.

entries.name: One
entries.body: The first block was mine to place, even without a finished plan. One reminds me of initiative and its lonely edge. What could a character begin, then invite others into?

entries.name: Two
entries.body: Two workbenches fit once we both moved our plans. Partnership needs a second voice and room for the first. Where could a character listen without simply giving way?

entries.name: Three
entries.body: The banner looked better when I showed someone my rough design. Three makes expression social. What idea could a character share before knowing how it will be received?

entries.name: Four
entries.body: Four corner posts let me build the roof without guessing. Reliable structure gives ordinary days support. Which modest habit would help a character keep their promises?

entries.name: Five
entries.body: I changed the path and found room for a workshop. Change can open things or scatter effort. Let a character try another way and notice what it asks them to give up.

entries.name: Six
entries.body: The supper table kept growing, but I had forgotten my own chair. Six holds the care of a household. How could a character include the caretaker among those who matter?

entries.name: Seven
entries.body: A quiet hour with my cave notes taught me more than another tunnel. Seven gives a question room. What might a character understand by staying instead of digging onward?

entries.name: Eight
entries.body: The trading hall worked when I counted more than my own profit. Eight gives resources consequences. How does a character use power others must live with?

entries.name: Nine
entries.body: Before leaving, I filled the shared chest and took only my tools. Nine lets a finished chapter serve others. What could a character release without claiming credit?

sections.title: Master Numbers
sections.intro: Modern numerology motifs: attention, lasting work and care passed onward.

entries.name: Eleven
entries.body: We heard a change in the tunnel and checked the wall together. Eleven sharpens Two's attention. An impression can start a character asking, without deciding the answer.

entries.name: Twenty-Two
entries.body: The long bridge needed a river-wide plan and joints I could fit by hand. Twenty-Two widens Four: what can a character build to carry people beyond their own days?

entries.name: Thirty-Three
entries.body: I opened the workshop so others could learn, then let them teach the next group. Thirty-Three widens Six's care. A skill can travel farther than one tired pair of hands.

closer.title: Leave a Light On
closer.body: The tools are away, and the cat has claimed my chair. Keep whatever helps your story. I've left another seat and a light for whoever comes home next.

postscript.title: A Small Clarification
postscript.body: I don't have to brag about the quality of mine. Unlike SOME people's guides out there.
